questions.phrase: Challenges the plausibility of X by offering Y as an alternative explanation.

options.text: Author defends X by giving Y as support.
Author attacks X by proposing Y as a different cause for whatever X tried to explain.
Author accepts X and Y as equally plausible.
Author cites Y as a definition of X.

questions.explanation: 'By offering' points to the tactic. The author challenges X by proposing a different cause Y. Alternative-explanation move.

questions.phrase: Substantiates the claim that X is false by demonstrating that Y is an inevitable consequence of X.

options.text: Author proves X by showing Y follows.
Author argues X must be false because Y would have to follow from X, and Y is unacceptable.
Author derives Y from X to support X.
Author rejects Y because X is true.

questions.explanation: Substantiates means supports. 'By demonstrating' marks the tactic. If Y inevitably follows from X and Y is unacceptable, X is false.

questions.phrase: Treats the occurrence of X as corroborating evidence for Y.

options.text: Y is the support, X is the conclusion.
X is the support, Y is the conclusion.
X and Y are both conclusions.
Neither X nor Y is support.

questions.explanation: 'Corroborating evidence for' tells you X supports Y. X is the evidence; Y is the conclusion.

questions.phrase: Generalizes from a single case, X, to a broad claim, Y.

options.text: Author concludes the broad claim Y on the basis of one example X.
Author rejects the broad claim Y because of one counterexample X.
Author defines Y in terms of X.
Author treats X as more important than Y.

questions.explanation: X is the single case (evidence). Y is the broad conclusion. Hasty-generalization pattern.

questions.phrase: Appeals to a general principle X to justify a particular decision Y.

options.text: Y is the rule; X is the case it justifies.
X is the rule; Y is the particular case the rule justifies.
X and Y are both rules.
Neither is a rule.

questions.explanation: General principle is the broad rule. 'To justify' points forward to the conclusion: the particular decision Y.

questions.phrase: Anticipates an objection by acknowledging X and then offering Y in response.

options.text: X is the author's own evidence; Y is the conclusion.
X is the concession or objection; Y is the response that addresses it.
X is the conclusion; Y is the evidence.
X and Y are independent claims.

questions.explanation: Anticipating an objection: X is the objection acknowledged, Y is the response the author uses to defuse it.

questions.phrase: Rejects X on the grounds that the proponents of X have a vested interest in its acceptance.

options.text: Author engages with the reasoning behind X.
Author attacks the motive of those who hold X rather than X itself.
Author concedes X and moves on.
Author supports X with new evidence.

questions.explanation: Classic ad hominem. The motive of the proponents is the attack, not the substance of X.

questions.flaw_description: Presumes, without providing justification, that a condition necessary for an outcome is also sufficient to produce that outcome.

model_answer.example: To win the lottery, you need to buy a ticket. I bought a ticket. Therefore I'll win the lottery.

questions.flaw_description: Mistakes a temporal relationship between two events for a causal relationship.

model_answer.logic_summary: Treats Y happening after X as proof that X caused Y.
model_answer.example: The rooster crowed, and then the sun came up. Therefore the rooster caused the sunrise.

questions.flaw_description: Rejects a position on the grounds that the proponents of the position have a vested interest in its acceptance.

model_answer.logic_summary: Ad hominem. Attacks the speaker's motive rather than the speaker's argument.
model_answer.example: The mechanic says my brakes need replacing, but he profits from the repair, so my brakes are fine.
